title: Sangrand: the first day of each Nanakshahi month, and the 2026–27 dates
desc: What Sangrand is, why Sikhs gather at the gurdwara on the first day of each month to hear the Barah Maha, and every Sangrand date of Nanakshahi 558.
alt: The Amrit Sarovar around Sri Harmandir Sahib in golden light
cap: The Amrit Sarovar at Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar
body: Sangrand is the first day of each month of the Nanakshahi calendar, the day on which the sun enters a new sign of the zodiac. The name comes from the Sanskrit sankranti, a passing over. There are twelve Sangrands in the year, and on each one many Sikhs go to the gurdwara in the morning to begin the new month in the Guru's presence.
## The Barah Maha

Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji holds two compositions called Barah Maha, songs of the twelve months: one by Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji in Raag Tukhari and one by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji in Raag Maajh. Each month's verses describe the season, the heat of Jeth, the rains of Sawan, the cold of Poh, and use it to speak of the soul's longing for the Divine. On Sangrand, gurdwaras read the verses for the new month, and the granthi announces the name of the month to the sangat.
## A Sikh view of the day

In the older Indian tradition, sankranti days were thought auspicious or inauspicious, and people bathed in holy rivers or gave alms to ward off ill fortune. The Gurus taught that no day is lucky or unlucky in itself, and that a day is blessed when the Divine is remembered in it. Sikhs keep Sangrand not as a ritual but as an occasion to listen to the Barah Maha and begin the month with Ardas. Some Sikh scholars discourage giving it special weight at all, and every day is equally the Guru's.
## How Sangrand is observed

Gurdwaras hold a morning programme of kirtan, the reading of the Barah Maha, katha and Ardas, followed by langar. Two Sangrands are also festivals: the Sangrand of Vaisakh is Vaisakhi, and the Sangrand of Magh is Maghi, the Jorh Mela at Sri Muktsar Sahib. The Sangrand of Chet is the Sikh New Year. Hazri shows every Sangrand in its calendar.

title: Masya: the new moon day, Tarn Taran Sahib, and the 2026–27 dates
desc: What Masya, the new moon day, means in Sikh practice, why sangats gather at Tarn Taran Sahib and other gurdwaras, and every Masya date of Nanakshahi 558.
body: Masya is the day of the new moon, when the moon cannot be seen, and it comes once in every lunar month, about every twenty-nine and a half days. In the Nanakshahi calendar for 558 there are twelve. In Punjab it is a day when large sangats gather at certain historic gurdwaras.
## Masya in Punjab

In Indian tradition the new moon, amavas, was long kept as a day for bathing in sacred waters, remembering ancestors and giving alms. Sikh tradition has kept the gathering but changed its meaning. On Masya, sangats travel to gurdwaras associated with the Gurus to hear kirtan and to bathe in the sarovar, and the best known of these gatherings is at Sri Darbar Sahib, Tarn Taran, the town founded by Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, whose sarovar is among the largest of all. Gurdwaras at Goindwal Sahib, Khadur Sahib, Baba Bakala and many other places also draw great numbers. At Sri Muktsar Sahib and Chheharta Sahib, a monthly Masya mela is a long tradition.
## What the Gurus taught

The Gurus taught that bathing at a holy place does not wash away the dirt of the mind, and that the true pilgrimage is to bathe in the Name. Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji questioned those who thought a dip at a particular moment could earn merit. Sikhs who keep Masya do so as a day to be in the sangat and to remember the Divine, not out of belief that the new moon itself is holy.
## How Masya is observed

Gurdwaras that keep the day hold kirtan from early morning, katha and Ardas, and serve langar to the large sangats. Many families make Masya their monthly visit to a historic gurdwara near them. Hazri lists every Masya in its calendar.

title: Puranmashi: the full moon day in the Sikh calendar, and the 2026–27 dates
desc: What Puranmashi, the full moon, means for Sikhs: the Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, monthly gatherings and Sukhmani Sahib, and every full moon date of Nanakshahi 558.
body: Puranmashi is the day of the full moon, which comes once in every lunar month. In the Nanakshahi calendar for 558 there are eleven, from April 2026 to February 2027. For many Sikhs it is a day to gather in the sangat, and one full moon in particular is the most celebrated day of the Sikh year.
## The full moon of Katak

The Prakash Purab of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Guru Nanak Gurpurab, is celebrated on the full moon of the month of Katak, which is why its date moves each year. On that night, gurdwaras are lit, and many Sikhs keep a vigil of kirtan into the night. Several other days are also tied to the full moon in Sikh tradition, among them Rakhar Puniya, the full moon of Sawan, when the Jorh Mela at Baba Bakala Sahib is held. Read about [Guru Nanak Dev Ji's Prakash Purab](/gurpurab/prakash-purab-guru-nanak-dev-ji).
## Puranmashi in the gurdwara

Many gurdwaras, especially in villages and towns of Punjab, hold a special programme every Puranmashi, often a Sukhmani Sahib paath, kirtan and Ardas in the evening, with langar. Some sangats complete a Sahaj Paath or an Akhand Paath each month on the full moon. In the old Punjab the full moon gave light for travel at night, and the custom of gathering on Puranmashi may have grown from that.
## What the Gurus taught
As with Sangrand and Masya, the Gurus taught that no day is holy in itself, and that what makes any day blessed is remembering the Divine. Sikhs who keep Puranmashi keep it as a time for the sangat.
## How Puranmashi is observed
Gurdwaras hold kirtan, Sukhmani Sahib, katha and Ardas. Hazri shows every Puranmashi in its calendar.
